zh.title: 目犍連的一生
zh.seo_title: 目犍連是誰？神通第一大弟子的一生與死亡（附經文出處）
zh.seo_description: 目犍連（Moggallāna）是佛陀的第二大弟子，以神通第一著稱。本頁依《巴利專有名詞辭典》（DPPN）與《思量經》（MN15）、《無穢經》（MN5）、《諦分別經》（MN141）巴利原典，整理他的出家因緣、神通事蹟、與舍利弗的友誼，以及關於他的死亡與「目犍連救母」故事的出處說明——每一段敘述都標明具名出處，可點入站內經文逐段對照。
zh.question: 目犍連是誰？
zh.definition: 目犍連（Moggallāna），全名大目犍連（Mahāmoggallāna），是佛陀的第二大弟子。依《巴利專有名詞辭典》（DPPN），他與摯友舍利弗一同出家，受戒後第七天證得阿羅漢，以神通第一著稱，在佛陀入滅前先行去世——而早期經典並沒有記載他死亡的情形。

sections.heading: 他是誰：神通第一的大弟子
paragraphs: 依《巴利專有名詞辭典》（DPPN），目犍連（Moggallāna）是喬達摩佛的第二大弟子（the second of the Chief Disciples）——第一位是舍利弗。DPPN 條目並列出他的另一個名字「拘律陀」（Kolita）。
DPPN 說，他的卓越之處在於神通（psychic power）：他能無數次變現出有生命的形體，也能隨意變成任何形貌。經中稱舍利弗與目犍連是理想的弟子，其他人應以他們為榜樣。
網路上關於目犍連的故事流傳極廣，但多數不附出處，也常把不同時代、不同傳統的材料混在一起講。本頁採取不同的做法：每一段敘述都具名標明來源——出自辭典的注明 DPPN，出自經文的直接引用站內巴利原典段落，可逐段點入對照；不在這些材料裡的故事，如實告訴你「它不在」。

sections.heading: 出家因緣：與舍利弗同行，七天證阿羅漢
paragraphs: 依 DPPN，目犍連與舍利弗最初一同在刪闍耶（Sañjaya）門下修行。後來舍利弗在王舍城遇見馬勝比丘（Assaji），聽聞「諸法因緣生」（ye dhammā hetuppabhavā）的偈頌而證得入流；他找到目犍連，向他複述這首偈，目犍連也隨之證得入流。
兩人先試著說服老師刪闍耶同行未果，便前往竹林精舍（Veḷuvana）拜見佛陀；刪闍耶門下五百名弟子同意隨行。佛陀為他們說法，並以「來吧，比丘們」為他們授戒。
接下來是 DPPN 記載中最動人的一幕：目犍連前往摩揭陀的迦拉瓦拉村（Kallavāla），受戒後第七天，禪坐中昏沉襲來。佛陀知道了，出現在他面前，勉勵他精勤。就在那一天，他證得阿羅漢。從聽聞一偈到證得究竟，前後只有短短數日——這是 DPPN 對他修行歷程的完整交代。

sections.heading: 「神通第一」是什麼樣子：DPPN 記載的事蹟
paragraphs: DPPN 條目收錄了多起神通展示的實例，每一則都附巴利文獻出處。其一：佛陀與比丘們在毗蘭若（Verañja）乞食不得時，目犍連提議把大地翻轉過來，讓地底的養分成為食物，又提議開一條路讓比丘們去他方乞食——兩項提議都被佛陀拒絕了（Vin.iii.7）。

其二：一群比丘坐在鹿母講堂樓下高談闊論、輕浮散漫，全然不顧佛陀就在樓上。佛陀囑意之下，目犍連用大腳趾撼動整座講堂，使它震響，以警醒他們（SN.v.269ff.）。其三：他去探望帝釋（Sakka），發現對方沉溺於自身的榮華而驕慢，便撼動帝釋的最勝宮（Vejayanta），使帝釋毛髮直豎、憍慢頓消（MN.i.251ff.）。他也曾上梵天界，當眾質問婆迦梵天（Baka Brahmā），使其承認先前的見解錯誤。
DPPN 還記載：魔羅（Māra）曾鑽進目犍連的腹中作祟，被他喝令出來——目犍連並告訴魔羅，自己在過去世也曾是一個名叫杜西（Dūsī）的魔（MN.i.332ff.，《魔訶責經》）。他能看見一般人肉眼不可見的餓鬼與眾生（SN.ii.254ff.）；諸天很歡迎他造訪天界（SN.v.366f.）。
值得注意的是這些記載的共同輪廓：依 DPPN，他的神通多用於教學與警策——喚醒散漫的比丘、折服驕慢的天神與梵天——而動用神通解決民生問題的提議，則被佛陀否決。

sections.heading: 佛陀怎麼評價他：《諦分別經》的「生母與養母」
paragraphs: DPPN 引《諦分別經》（MN141，MN.iii.248）記載佛陀如何區分這對「雙賢弟子」：「舍利弗如同生產者，目犍連如同養育所生者的乳母；舍利弗訓練人證入流果，目犍連訓練人達到最高義。」這段話在站內經文中有完整的現場紀錄。
《諦分別經》開頭，佛陀在鹿野苑向比丘眾略說四聖諦後，當眾勸大家親近舍利弗與目犍連，稱他們是智慧的比丘、同修梵行者的扶助者。「生母與養母」的分工是一個很具體的評價：舍利弗把人領進聖道之流，目犍連則陪人走到終點——最高義，即阿羅漢的究竟解脫。
DPPN 也記載佛陀對他說法能力的直接肯定：有一次佛陀在迦毘羅衛的新講堂為釋迦族人說法後疲倦了，便請目犍連接著為比丘們開示；目犍連講說貪欲與離貪之道，說畢，佛陀熱切地稱讚了他（SN.iv.183ff.）。

sections.heading: 教學現場：《思量經》（MN15）——他教比丘如何自省
paragraphs: 說起目犍連，多數人只記得神通；但站內保存了一部他親自說法的經——《思量經》（MN15）。在跋祇國鱷魚山的鹿野苑，他召集比丘，開示一個與神通無關、卻極其實用的主題：怎樣的人聽得進勸，怎樣的人聽不進，以及如何檢查自己是哪一種。
他先列出十六種「使人難以教誡的法」——惡欲、自讚毀他、易怒懷恨、被指責就反擊、固守己見……接著給出方法：先「以自己推知自己」，看見別人有這些特質時令人不喜，便推知自己若有，同樣令人不喜；再逐條「以自己省察自己」，查到了就精進捨斷，查無此事就歡喜地繼續修學。
開示的結尾，他給了一個著名的譬喻：如同愛好裝扮的年輕人在明鏡或清水中照看自己的臉，見到污點就設法除去，不見污點就歡喜。這部經呈現的目犍連，是一位務實而體貼的老師——這與 DPPN 的記載一致：佛陀交付他照看比丘們的福祉，他也勤勉地履行；《長老偈》中留有多首他勸勉同修的偈頌，甚至有一次他親手把行為不端的比丘架出門外、閂上門（AN.iv.204ff.）。

sections.heading: 與舍利弗：《無穢經》裡的一場對答
paragraphs: 依 DPPN，目犍連與舍利弗之間的情誼與敬重是相互的：《長老偈》中舍利弗讚歎目犍連的偈頌（Thag.1178–1181），甚至比目犍連讚歎舍利弗的更為動人。兩人最深的聯繫是對佛陀共同的愛；分隔兩地時，他們會以天耳與天眼相通，互相分享各自與佛陀的談話（SN.ii.275ff.）。提婆達多分裂僧團、帶走五百比丘時，佛陀派去把人帶回來的，正是舍利弗與目犍連兩人——他們成功完成了任務（Vin.ii.185）。
站內的《無穢經》（MN5）保存了兩人搭檔說法的現場。舍利弗提出「有垢知垢、無垢知垢」四種人的分類後，目犍連立刻追問：同樣有垢的兩人，為什麼一個被稱為劣、一個被稱為勝？這一問把整部經的核心引了出來，舍利弗於是展開銅缽的譬喻，層層作答。
經的末段，目犍連以自己在王舍城親眼所見的一幕作譬：車匠之子削製車輪的輪緣，旁觀的老車匠心中想著「削去這個彎、這個歪、這個瑕疵就好了」，車匠之子便恰恰削去那些地方——他讚歎舍利弗的說法正是如此，宛如知曉他人的心，從心刨心。經文以「那兩位大士彼此隨喜對方所善說的話語」作結。

sections.heading: 目犍連之死：早期經典其實怎麼說
paragraphs: 網路上「目犍連之死」的故事版本很多——被外道雇兇圍毆、骨碎而亡、宿世業報成熟等等，講得繪聲繪影。在複述任何版本之前，值得先看本頁所據材料的原話。

依 DPPN：舍利弗先於目犍連去世，《長老偈》保存了數首目犍連悼念舍利弗之死的偈頌（Thag.1158–1161）；目犍連顯然在佛陀之前去世，因為《相應部》記有佛陀提及兩人皆已離世。然後是關鍵的一句——「然而，早期經典並沒有留下關於目犍連死亡情形的記載」（the early texts contain no record of the circumstances of Moggallāna's death）。
也就是說：就巴利經藏與律藏這一層最早的文獻而言，我們確知的只有他去世的相對時序——在舍利弗之後、佛陀之前。坊間流傳的遇害情節與業報解釋，並不出自這一層文獻，也不在本頁所據的 DPPN 節錄與站內經文之中；本頁依出處紀律不予複述，也不評斷其真偽。若你在別處讀到那些故事，可以帶著這個座標去讀：它們屬於更晚的傳述層，而非早期經典。

zh.mahayana_note: 許多讀者搜尋「目犍連」，其實是想找「目連救母」——目犍連以神通見亡母墮餓鬼道、依佛陀指示於僧自恣日供養眾僧以救度母親的故事，也就是盂蘭盆節（農曆七月十五）的由來。需要如實說明的是：這個故事出自漢傳佛教所傳的《盂蘭盆經》，屬於漢傳文獻傳統；在巴利傳統中，《巴利專有名詞辭典》（DPPN）的目犍連條目並沒有救母的記載——巴利材料中與之相近的元素，只有他「能看見餓鬼與諸趣眾生」的能力（SN.ii.254ff.）。兩個傳統各自傳承了不同的目犍連敘事：巴利經藏側重他的神通、教學與護持僧團，漢傳的救母故事則發展出影響深遠的孝道與超度文化。本站依巴利原典呈現前者，漢傳傳統的故事並陳於此供對照，不作真偽裁決。

faq.a: 依《巴利專有名詞辭典》（DPPN）：舍利弗先去世，目犍連隨後、在佛陀入滅之前去世；《長老偈》保存了他悼念舍利弗的偈頌。至於死亡的情形，DPPN 明言「早期經典並沒有留下記載」。網路上流傳的被外道雇兇襲擊、宿業成熟等情節，不出自巴利經藏這一層早期文獻，也不在本頁所據材料之中，故本頁不複述、不裁決。

faq.q: 目犍連救母（盂蘭盆）是真的嗎？
faq.a: 這要看你問的是哪個文獻傳統。「目連救母」出自漢傳佛教所傳的《盂蘭盆經》，是盂蘭盆節的由來，在漢傳文化中影響深遠。巴利傳統方面，DPPN 的目犍連條目沒有救母的記載；巴利材料中相近的元素，只有他能看見餓鬼等一般人不可見的眾生（SN.ii.254ff.）。兩個傳統各有其傳承，本站依巴利原典呈現，並陳而不裁決。

faq.q: 目犍連和舍利弗是什麼關係？
faq.a: 依 DPPN，兩人是至交：一同在刪闍耶門下修行，舍利弗聽聞馬勝比丘的偈頌證入流後，第一件事就是找目犍連複述，然後兩人一同投入佛陀座下。佛陀在《諦分別經》（MN141）中以「生母與養母」並舉兩人：舍利弗引人證入流果，目犍連引人達到最高義。DPPN 說兩人的情誼與敬重是相互的，分隔兩地時會以天耳天眼相通問候。《無穢經》（MN5）保存了兩人一問一答、互相隨喜的說法現場。

faq.q: 目犍連「神通第一」是什麼意思？
faq.a: 依 DPPN（引 AN.i.23），目犍連在佛陀弟子中的卓越之處（pre-eminence）在於神通：能無數次變現有生命的形體、隨意改變形貌。DPPN 收錄的實例包括：以腳趾撼動鹿母講堂警醒散漫的比丘（SN.v.269ff.）、撼動帝釋的最勝宮以折服其驕慢（MN.i.251ff.）、在梵天界當眾質問婆迦梵天使其認錯，以及能看見餓鬼等不可見的眾生。值得注意的是，這些神通多用於教學與警策；而他提議用神通解決飢荒乞食問題時，被佛陀拒絕了（Vin.iii.7）。

站內目前可逐段對照閱讀的是《思量經》（MN15）：他教比丘先「以自己推知自己」、再逐條省察自己是否有惡欲、易怒、固守己見等十六種難以受教的特質，並以照鏡譬喻作結，附巴利原文與白話對照。另依 DPPN，《相應部》等處還記有他多次說法：佛陀疲倦時請他代講貪欲與離貪之道（SN.iv.183ff.）、講禪那與導向解脫的特質（SN.iv.262–269），帝釋與諸天也曾專程來聽他說法。他在《無穢經》（MN5）中與舍利弗的對答亦可在站內閱讀。

en.title: The Life of Moggallana
en.seo_title: Who Was Moggallana? The Buddha's Disciple Foremost in Psychic Power — A Sourced Life and Death
en.seo_description: Moggallana (Mahāmoggallāna) was the second chief disciple of the Buddha, famed for his psychic powers. This page assembles his life strictly from named sources — the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (DPPN) and the Pali suttas MN 15, MN 5, and MN 141 — including what the early texts actually say (and do not say) about his death and the 'Moggallana saves his mother' story.
en.question: Who was Moggallana?
en.definition: Moggallana (Pali: Moggallāna, honorifically Mahāmoggallāna) was the second of the two chief disciples of the Buddha. According to the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (DPPN), he went forth together with his great friend Sāriputta, attained arahantship on the seventh day after his ordination, was pre-eminent in psychic power, and died before the Buddha — while the early texts contain no record of the circumstances of his death.

sections.heading: Who He Was: The Disciple Foremost in Psychic Power
paragraphs: According to the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (DPPN), Moggallāna was the second of the Chief Disciples of Gotama Buddha — the first being Sāriputta. The DPPN entry also gives his other name, Kolita.

His pre-eminence, the DPPN says, lay in his possession of psychic power: he could create a living shape innumerable times and could transform himself into any shape at will. The suttas declare Sāriputta and Moggallāna to be the ideal disciples whose example others should follow.

Stories about Moggallana circulate widely online, mostly without sources, and often blending materials from different eras and traditions. This page takes the opposite approach: every statement is attributed by name — to the DPPN, or to Pali sutta passages on this site that you can open and check segment by segment — and where a famous story is absent from these materials, we say so plainly.

sections.heading: How He Went Forth: With Sāriputta, to Arahantship in Seven Days
paragraphs: According to the DPPN, Moggallāna and Sāriputta first practiced together as disciples of Sañjaya. Later, Sāriputta, wandering in Rājagaha, met Assaji, heard the stanza 'ye dhammā hetuppabhavā' ('of things that arise from a cause...'), and became a stream-enterer; he found Moggallāna and repeated the stanza to him, and Moggallāna too became a stream-enterer.

After an unsuccessful attempt to persuade their teacher Sañjaya to come along, the two set out for the Buddha at Veḷuvana — and Sañjaya's five hundred disciples agreed to go with them. The Buddha preached to them and ordained them with the words 'Come, monks.'

Then comes the most striking scene in the DPPN's account: Moggallāna went to the hamlet of Kallavāla in Magadha, and on the seventh day after his ordination, drowsiness overcame him as he sat meditating. The Buddha knew this, appeared before him, and exhorted him to be zealous. That very day he attained arahantship. From hearing a single stanza to the final goal took only days — and that is the DPPN's complete account of his path.

sections.heading: What 'Foremost in Psychic Power' Looked Like: Episodes from the DPPN
paragraphs: The DPPN entry records several displays of iddhi (psychic power), each with its Pali source. One: when the Buddha and his monks failed to get alms in Verañja, Moggallāna offered to turn the earth upside down so that the nutritive essence on its under surface might serve as food, and offered to open a road so the monks could go elsewhere for alms — both offers were refused by the Buddha (Vin.iii.7).

Two: when some monks sat on the ground floor of the Migāramātupāsāda talking loosely and frivolously, heedless of the Buddha in the upper story, Moggallāna, at the Buddha's request, shook the whole building with his great toe and made it rattle to shake them awake (SN.v.269ff.). Three: visiting Sakka, king of the gods, and finding him obsessed with his own splendour, Moggallāna shook Sakka's palace Vejayanta until Sakka's hair stood on end and his pride was humbled (MN.i.251ff.). He also went to the Brahma world and questioned Baka Brahmā in solemn conclave, making him confess that his earlier views were erroneous.

The DPPN further records that Māra once worried Moggallāna by entering his belly — Moggallāna ordered him out, and told him that he himself had once, in a past life, been a Māra named Dūsī (MN.i.332ff., the Māratajjanīya Sutta). He could see petas (hungry ghosts) and other beings invisible to the ordinary eye (SN.ii.254ff.), and his visits to the deva worlds were very welcome to the devas (SN.v.366f.).

Notice the common shape of these episodes: in the DPPN's account, his powers serve teaching and admonition — waking up heedless monks, humbling proud gods and Brahmās — while his one proposal to solve a subsistence problem by psychic power was turned down by the Buddha.

sections.heading: How the Buddha Rated Him: 'Mother and Nurse' in MN 141
paragraphs: The DPPN cites the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta (MN 141, MN.iii.248) for the Buddha's way of distinguishing these 'twin brethren': 'Sāriputta is as she who brings forth and Moggallāna is as the nurse of what is brought forth; Sāriputta trains in the fruits of conversion, Moggallāna trains in the highest good.' The full scene is preserved in the sutta on this site.

At the opening of MN 141, after briefly stating the four noble truths at the Deer Park, the Buddha publicly urges the monks to associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, calling them wise monks who assist their fellow practitioners. The 'mother and nurse' division of labour is a concrete appraisal: Sāriputta brings people into the stream of the noble path; Moggallāna walks with them to the end — the highest goal, the final liberation of the arahant.

The DPPN also records the Buddha's direct compliment to Moggallāna's preaching: once, having himself taught the Sakyans in their new Mote Hall at Kapilavatthu, the weary Buddha asked Moggallāna to talk to the monks; Moggallāna spoke of lusts and the means of getting rid of them, and at the end of the sermon the Buddha praised him warmly (SN.iv.183ff.).

sections.heading: In the Classroom: The Anumāna Sutta (MN 15) — Teaching Monks to Examine Themselves
paragraphs: Most people remember only the psychic powers; but this site preserves a discourse Moggallāna delivered himself — the Anumāna Sutta, 'Measuring in Accordance' (MN 15). At the Deer Park on Crocodile Hill among the Bhaggas, he gathers the monks and teaches a subject that has nothing to do with iddhi and everything to do with daily practice: what makes a person easy or hard to admonish, and how to check which one you are.

He first lists sixteen qualities that make a person hard to admonish — corrupt wishes, exalting oneself and disparaging others, anger and resentment, striking back when reproved, clinging obstinately to one's own views. Then comes the method: first infer about yourself from others — seeing how unlikable these qualities are in another, infer that you would be just as unlikable with them; then review yourself item by item, striving to abandon whatever you find, and dwelling glad and joyful, training day and night in wholesome qualities, whenever you find yourself clear.

He closes with a famous simile: like a young person fond of adornment examining their own face in a bright mirror or a bowl of clear water — removing any dirt or blemish they see, and rejoicing if they see none. The Moggallāna of this sutta is a practical, considerate teacher — consistent with the DPPN's record that the Buddha charged him with looking after the monks' welfare, a charge he carried out diligently; the Theragāthā preserves several of his verses exhorting his colleagues, and on one occasion he personally seized a badly behaved monk, thrust him outside, and bolted the door (AN.iv.204ff.).

sections.heading: With Sāriputta: A Dialogue in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta (MN 5)
paragraphs: According to the DPPN, the love between Moggallāna and Sāriputta was mutual, as was the admiration: Sāriputta's verses in praise of Moggallāna in the Theragāthā (Thag.1178–1181) are even more eloquent than Moggallāna's in praise of Sāriputta. Their strongest bond was the love of each for the Buddha; when apart, they would relate to each other, by means of the divine ear and the divine eye, how they had been conversing with him (SN.ii.275ff.). When Devadatta split the Sangha and led five hundred monks away, it was Sāriputta and Moggallāna whom the Buddha sent to bring them back — and they succeeded (Vin.ii.185).

The Anaṅgaṇa Sutta (MN 5) on this site preserves the two working in tandem. After Sāriputta sets out his fourfold classification of persons — with or without inner blemish, knowing it or not — Moggallāna immediately asks the driving question: of two people equally blemished, why is one called inferior and the other superior? That question draws out the heart of the discourse, and Sāriputta answers layer by layer with the simile of the bronze bowl.

At the end of the sutta, Moggallāna offers a scene he had witnessed himself in Rājagaha: a cartwright's son planing the rim of a wheel while an old cartwright looks on, thinking 'if only he would plane off this bend, this twist, this flaw' — and the young man planes off exactly those places. Sāriputta's teaching, Moggallāna says in praise, is just like that: as if knowing heart from heart, he planes the heart. The sutta closes with the two great beings rejoicing in each other's well-spoken words.

sections.heading: The Death of Moggallana: What the Early Texts Actually Say
paragraphs: Versions of 'the death of Moggallana' abound online — beaten by hired assassins, his bones crushed, the ripening of ancient kamma — told in vivid detail. Before repeating any of them, it is worth reading what the materials this page relies on actually say.

According to the DPPN: Sāriputta died before Moggallāna, and the Theragāthā contains several verses attributed to Moggallāna on Sāriputta's death (Thag.1158–1161); Moggallāna evidently died before the Buddha, as the Saṃyutta Nikāya records the Buddha speaking of both as dead. Then comes the key sentence: 'the early texts contain no record of the circumstances of Moggallāna's death.'

In other words: at the level of the earliest stratum — the Pali suttas and Vinaya — what we can confirm is only the relative timing of his passing: after Sāriputta, before the Buddha. The widely told assassination scenes and their karmic explanations do not come from this stratum, and are not in the materials this page relies on (the DPPN excerpt and the suttas on this site); in keeping with this page's sourcing discipline, we neither retell them nor rule on their truth. If you meet those stories elsewhere, you can read them with this coordinate in hand: they belong to a later layer of transmission, not to the early canon.

en.mahayana_note: Many readers searching for Moggallana are really looking for 'Mulian saves his mother' — the story in which Moggallana sees with his psychic powers that his late mother has fallen among the hungry ghosts, and, on the Buddha's instruction, rescues her by making offerings to the Sangha at the end of the rains retreat. This is the origin story of the Ullambana (Ghost) Festival, held on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month across East Asia. It should be stated plainly: this story comes from the Ullambana Sutra as transmitted in the Chinese Buddhist tradition; in the Pali tradition, the DPPN entry on Moggallāna contains no account of him saving his mother — the nearest element in the Pali materials is his ability to see petas (hungry ghosts) and other beings invisible to the ordinary eye (SN.ii.254ff.). The two traditions each transmit a different Moggallana narrative: the Pali canon emphasizes his psychic power, his teaching, and his guardianship of the Sangha, while the Chinese story of saving his mother grew into a profoundly influential culture of filial devotion and rites for the departed. This site presents the former from the Pali sources, and sets the Chinese tradition's story alongside for comparison, without ruling on its truth.

faq.a: According to the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (DPPN): Sāriputta died first, and Moggallāna died after him but before the Buddha; the Theragāthā preserves his verses mourning Sāriputta. As for the circumstances of his death, the DPPN states plainly that 'the early texts contain no record.' The widely circulated accounts of hired assassins and ripening kamma do not come from the early Pali stratum and are not in the materials this page relies on, so this page neither retells them nor rules on them.

faq.q: Is the story of Moggallana saving his mother (Ullambana) true?
faq.a: It depends on which textual tradition you are asking about. 'Mulian saves his mother' comes from the Ullambana Sutra of the Chinese Buddhist tradition and is the origin of the Ghost Festival, deeply influential in East Asian culture. On the Pali side, the DPPN entry on Moggallāna contains no such account; the nearest element in the Pali materials is his ability to see hungry ghosts and other beings invisible to ordinary eyes (SN.ii.254ff.). Each tradition has its own transmission; this site presents the Pali sources and sets the two side by side without a verdict.

faq.q: What was Moggallana's relationship with Sāriputta?
faq.a: According to the DPPN, the two were the closest of friends: they practiced together under Sañjaya, and when Sāriputta attained stream-entry on hearing Assaji's stanza, the first thing he did was find Moggallāna and repeat it — after which the two joined the Buddha together. In MN 141 the Buddha pairs them as 'mother and nurse': Sāriputta guides people to stream-entry, Moggallāna to the highest goal. The DPPN says their love and admiration were mutual, and that when apart they kept in touch by the divine ear and divine eye. MN 5 preserves a live scene of the two teaching in tandem and rejoicing in each other's words.

faq.q: What does 'foremost in psychic power' mean?
faq.a: According to the DPPN (citing AN.i.23), Moggallāna's pre-eminence among the Buddha's disciples lay in psychic power: he could create living shapes innumerable times and transform himself at will. Recorded examples include shaking the Migāramātupāsāda with his toe to wake up frivolous monks (SN.v.269ff.), shaking Sakka's palace Vejayanta to humble the god's pride (MN.i.251ff.), publicly questioning Baka Brahmā in the Brahma world until he admitted his views were wrong, and seeing hungry ghosts invisible to ordinary eyes. Notably, these powers served teaching and admonition — while his offer to solve a famine by turning the earth over was refused by the Buddha (Vin.iii.7).

On this site you can read the Anumāna Sutta (MN 15) segment by segment: he teaches the monks to infer about themselves from others and to review themselves item by item for sixteen qualities that make a person hard to admonish, closing with the mirror simile — with Pali text and translation side by side. According to the DPPN, the Saṃyutta Nikāya and other collections record further sermons: he taught on lusts and the means of getting rid of them when the Buddha was weary (SN.iv.183ff.), and on the jhānas and the qualities leading to true emancipation (SN.iv.262–269); Sakka and other gods came in person to hear him preach. His dialogue with Sāriputta in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta (MN 5) can also be read on this site.
